rv.q: What her revision has set out to undo isn’t actually Macbeth: It’s generations of facile discourse around Shakespeare’s play, discourse that’s all too apt to be equated with the play itself.
Harris’s work with the actors, especially, fittingly, the women, stays strong.
Subpar design and a shaggy script contribute to the flagging momentum of the play as it ambles past the two-hour mark.
While Zinnie Harris’ Macbeth (an undoing) lives up to its name, it seems rather unnecessary as it mostly flips the genders rather than tell us anything new.
If Macbeth (an undoing) is a near-miss, it is elegantly appointed and filled with people worth knowing.
The ringing answer could be, “Not a lot.”

But Cooper is as charismatic as her character is quixotic, a riveting onstage presence as she grapples with the felonious path she has chosen for her and her husband to assume power — and how the consequences for her are even weightier given her gender.

But while Harris succeeds in expanding Lady Macbeth’s presence in the story, ultimately the playwright is defeated in increasing the character’s agency, given Shakespeare’s clear-cut trajectory of the doomed Queen.
It’s a lovely ending to a tragic story.

cn.t: This feminist reimagining of Macbeth centering Lady Macbeth's story draws mixed reviews, with critics finding the concept intriguing but the execution unfocused and confused, resulting in a haphazard adaptation that struggles to justify its reworking.
